title: Bird community temperature index followed less than 10% of May-July warming on 5,294 North American survey routes in 1970-2024 with route and observer controls
abstract: Question: did breeding bird communities in Canada and the United States change toward warm-adapted species as fast as the breeding season became warmer? Approach: we used 124,128 standard North American Breeding Bird Survey runs (5,294 routes, 1970-2024) and NOAA GHCN_CAMS gridded temperature. We calculated a cross-fitted Species Temperature Index for 432 species per route half and a Community Temperature Index (CTI) for each run. Fixed-effects models with route and observer effects and two-way clustered errors gave the CTI and temperature trends on the same route-years. Results: the CTI increased by 0.015 C per decade (95% CI 0.007 to 0.023), and May-July temperature increased by 0.249 C per decade (0.177 to 0.322). The tracking ratio was 0.061 (0.029 to 0.093), with almost the same value in the East and the West. All nine sensitivity variants gave less than 10% tracking. The CTI decreased in 1970-1996 (-0.029 C per decade) and increased in 1997-2024 (+0.052; tracking ratio 0.14). Across 27 to 30 Bird Conservation Regions, faster warming did not give faster CTI increase (1997-2024 slope -0.084, SE 0.047). Declines of warm farmland and grassland species (Northern Bobwhite, Eastern Meadowlark) and increases of warm woodland species (Turkey Vulture, Red-bellied Woodpecker, Carolina Wren) controlled the CTI changes. Observation bias: without observer effects, the 1970-2024 CTI trend was 0.001 C per decade, and CTI increased by 0.009 C per 10 years of observer tenure. Limitations: interpolated 0.5 degree temperature, no detection model, temperature-only species niches, and BCR temperature errors not in the cross-region slope. Conclusion: communities have a large climate debt of about 0.23 C per decade, but the CTI changes that occurred are not clear evidence of a climate response.

display.caption: Annual May-July temperature anomaly (top, route fixed effects) and Community Temperature Index anomaly (bottom, route and observer fixed effects) for East and West BBS routes, 1970-2024. The dotted line marks the pre-chosen 1996/1997 period split. Note the different y-axis scales: temperature rose about 1 C, the CTI about 0.1 C.

Left: CTI trends (circles) and temperature trends (squares) per decade with 95% CIs, by region and period. Right: tracking ratio (CTI trend / temperature trend) with delta-method 95% CIs; 1 is full tracking. Errors are two-way clustered by route and year.

Left and centre: CTI trend against temperature trend for Bird Conservation Regions with at least 40 routes, 1970-1996 and 1997-2024 (bars: 95% CI of CTI trend; solid line: random-effects weighted fit; dashed line: full tracking). Right: trends of summed log(1+count) of the cold, middle and warm thirds of species by STI, as percent of the mean per decade.
